A fixed dose of isoniazid is given to a group of 200 healthy volunteers.  Plasma drug concentration is measured 4 hours later, and a histogram of the observed results is shown below.

Variation in which of the following processes best explains the bimodal rather than unimodal distribution of plasma concentrations?​‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​​​​​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​​‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌​​
explanation:
In this experiment, a fixed oral dose of isoniazid (INH) is followed by measurement of plasma drug concentration at a set time, and the results are plotted as a histogram.

Most metabolic processes vary continuously across a population, reflecting the combined influence of many genetic and environmental factors.  Plasma concentrations after a fixed dose therefore cluster around a single population mean, producing a unimodal, roughly bell-shaped distribution.  A bimodal distribution suggests that the population contains 2 subgroups with different rates of drug clearance; INH classically produces this pattern because of genetically determined differences in acetylation.

INH is acetylated by N-acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2), a cytosolic hepatic enzyme that also metabolizes other drugs containing aromatic amine or hydrazine groups (eg, dapsone, hydralazine, procainamide).  Polymorphisms in the NAT2 gene divide the population into fast and slow acetylators, which correspond to the lower- and higher-concentration peaks on the histogram, respectively.

Slow acetylators clear INH more slowly, and the resulting accumulation increases the risk of adverse effects (eg, peripheral neuropathy).  Likewise, hydralazine and procainamide have a higher risk of causing drug-induced lupus in slow acetylators.  In contrast, fast acetylators clear INH more rapidly and may require higher doses to reach therapeutic concentrations.

(Choice B)  Amine oxidation is performed by monoamine oxidases (MAOs) and cytochrome P450 enzymes.  MAOs metabolize neurotransmitters and are the target of MAO inhibitors used in depression and Parkinson disease.  MAO-mediated oxidation is not a significant route of INH clearance.

(Choice C)  Glucuronidation conjugates fat-soluble drugs (eg, morphine, acetaminophen, lorazepam) and endogenous bilirubin to water-soluble forms for elimination.  However, glucuronidation is not the principal pathway responsible for INH clearance.

(Choice D)  Hydrolysis is carried out by esterases and amidases and participates in INH metabolism downstream of acetylation, but it does not contribute to the bimodal distribution of INH metabolism.  Clinically important polymorphisms include atypical plasma cholinesterase (prolongs the action of succinylcholine).

(Choice E)  Methylation inactivates catecholamines (catechol-O-methyltransferase) and thiopurines such as azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine.  Thiopurine methyltransferase deficiency causes severe myelosuppression on standard thiopurine doses, but this pathway does not metabolize INH.

Educational objective:Isoniazid is metabolized by N-acetyltransferase 2, which exhibits a genetic polymorphism producing distinct fast and slow acetylator phenotypes.  Because the population divides into 2 discrete groups rather than varying continuously, plasma concentrations after a fixed dose form a bimodal distribution.  Slow acetylators accumulate isoniazid and are at increased risk for adverse effects such as peripheral neuropathy.​‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​​​​​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​​‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌​​
